newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's new phone operator seen slashing prices.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's new phone operator seen slashing prices.

text.p: Portugal's third cellular phone operator, likely to be launched late next year after a bidding process, will slash prices to muscle into a rapidly growing market, analysts said on Thursday.

So far just one group, a consortium including state-run utility EDP-Electricidade de Portugal, industrial group Sonae, Maxitel, Transgas and Gas de Portugal, has said it will bid jointly for the licence.

Candidates must present bids by September 15 and a decision will be taken by the end of 1997. The third operator could be launched on the local market nine to 12 months after the licence is awarded, possibly by Christmas next year, analysts said.

The two present cellular phone operators in Portugal are Telecel-Comunicacoes Pessoais, which is 51 percent controlled by the European arm of the U.S. AirTouch Communications Inc, and TMN-Telecomunicacoes Moveis Nacionais, a subsidiary of state-controlled Portugal Telecom.
"When the third operator starts, there will be a price war, but not a very aggressive one," said Jose Freire of Espirito Santo Research.
He said the new entrant would offer a cut-price service in order to gain a foothold in the market, but it would not offer excessive discounts as it had to retain a viable long-term business plan.

James Golob of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London said: "A new operator in a cellular phone market must offer a competitive edge. The focus will be on the retail market, rather than the saturated business market."
He said that the third licence holder would probably offer a discounted package of services in order to woo customers.

Another London-based analyst, who asked not to be identified, said that the third operator would have to grab retail investors -- individuals and families -- as a priority as demand in the business segment was already heavy.
He said average revenue per user would continue to fall as growth came from individual clients rather than businesses.

According to the Financial Times Mobile Communications trade publication, 7.88 percent of the Portuguese population had cellular phones, compared with 8.71 percent in Spain, 12.4 percent in Britain and 10.5 percent in Europe on June 1, 1997. Scandinavian countries, which set up cellular networks relatively early, had penetration rates of at least 30 percent.
Freire said the penetration rate in Portugal could rise to 12 percent by the end of 1997. The London-based analyst estimated that it would climb to 20 percent by end-2000.
Analysts said they expected Portugal's cellular phone sector to grow strongly as it caught up with the fixed network in the coming years.
Freire said he forecast that Telecel could post a net profit of 13 billion escudos in 1997. He had no 1997 forecast for TMN.
Golob said TMN could post a 1997 net profit of between 11 and 12 billion escudos.

Telecel's six-month 1997 net profit, announced on Wednesday, surged by 127 percent year-on-year to 5.851 billion escudos, and TMN's six-month 1997 net profit rose by 183 percent to 5.72 billion escudos.
Despite falling tariffs, both operators managed to boost profits by widening their customer bases and offering successful pre-paid packages of services.
